title: Harvest festival
hookLine: churches fill with produce, loaves and tins for food banks

cards: A marrow the size of a small dog lies across the front of the altar.
Next to it, a basket of apples, a sheaf of wheat tied with string, a loaf baked in the shape of a wheatsheaf, and a pyramid of tinned tomatoes and baked beans leaning slightly to the left.
A child walks up the aisle holding a single carrot as if it were a crown. The church smells of bread and earth. On Monday, the tins go in a van to the food bank.
This is the harvest festival, and a harvest hymn sings that all good gifts around us are sent from heaven above.

teach.b: Harvest festival isn't a single date in the church calendar. Churches, schools and villages hold it when the crops are in, often on a Sunday in the autumn. But the idea under it runs through the Bible.
A psalm sings to God: "Thou crownest the year with thy goodness." The year has a crown, and the crown is food.
The letter of James puts it plainly: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights." The hymn's line, all good gifts, echoes it.
The food on the altar says: we didn't make this from nothing. Sun, rain, soil, seed, and a lot of other people's work came first. Then the second turn, just as old.
The law of Moses tells farmers not to strip their fields bare.

teach.h: LEAVE THE CORNERS OF THE FIELD.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest."

And if a farmer forgets a sheaf in the field, he's told not to go back for it: "it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow." The edges of the field belonged, by law, to the people with no field.
That's why the tins matter: they're the corners of the field, in a supermarket age. So the harvest festival does two things at once.
It looks up, in thanks. And it looks across, to the neighbor whose cupboard is empty.

how: Churches and schools hold harvest festivals when the crops are in, decorating the church with produce and bread, singing harvest hymns, and collecting tins and packets for food banks or local charities.

o: a market where the church sells produce for funds
a fixed feast day for blessing the first seeds sown
a church's thanksgiving for the crops, with food shared

games.q: what's on the altar — tap the pairs.
p: left for those with no field

s: harvest festival has one fixed date in the church calendar
churches, schools and villages hold it when the crops are in.
the law of Moses tells farmers to leave the corners of the field
and not to gather the gleanings, so the poor can.
"every good gift" comes from the Psalms
it's the letter of James. the Psalm says, thou crownest the year with thy goodness.

games.q: you're a farmer in the law of Moses. the harvest is in, and you notice one sheaf left lying in the field. what do you do?
o: leave it for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow.
games.why: the law says leave it: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow.

practice: Picture your own kitchen, the cupboard, the fridge, the shelf, and walk along it in your mind; pick one thing, a tin, a packet, a jar, that you could give away, something you'd be glad to eat yourself.
If you pray, give thanks for the people whose work put it on your shelf; if you don't, just hold them in mind: the grower, the picker, the driver.

wordCard.voice: Harvest festival. A church's thanksgiving for the crops, when the altar fills with food, and much of the food goes to people who need it.

carryVoice: Your line: all good gifts. The corners of the field still belong to someone. See you tomorrow.
